newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire threatens Rwanda-backed rebels with war.
newsitem.headline: Zaire threatens Rwanda-backed rebels with war.

text.p: Zaire said on Tuesday ethnic Tutsi rebels backed by neighbouring Rwanda had gained territory in the eastern region of Zaire, and gave them a week to leave or face fullscale war.

At a news conference in this eastern Zairean town shortly after attending a meeting of military officials from the capital Kinshasa, South Kivu deputy governor Lwasi Ngabo Lwabanji said the Banyamulenge Tutsis were bent on destabilising Zaire.
"The rebels came from Rwanda and they have gained Zairean territory. We will not accept to have two armies on the Zairean territory," Lwabanji said.

The deputy governor said the Banyamulenge rebels had attacked the town of Lemera mid-way between Bukavu and the city of Uvira on October 6, killing all patients and medical staff. He gave no death toll.
He said the rebels, together with 400,000 Banyamulenge civilians residing in the plateau area of South Kivu, had a week to leave or face all-out war from the Zairean defence forces.
The Zairean authorities want to concentrate the Banyamulenge in government-controlled camps to make them easier for the Zairean army to monitor.
Lwabanji said any Banyamulenge failing to heed his warning within seven days would be considered rebels and attacked by the Zairean army.
"We are opening a corridor for the Banyamulenge who want to get out for one week. After that whoever remains will be considered a rebel and will be treated as such," he said.
Lwabanji's no-nonsense news conference followed a high- level military meeting held in Bukavu on Tuesday by high ranking generals from headquarters in Kinshasa.
Residents in the region had earlier said Zairean soldiers went on a rampage in Uvira in the early hours of Tuesday.

The region had already been tense because of a growing conflict between the Zairean army and the Banyamulenge people, ethnic Tutsis who went there about 200 years ago from what are today Rwanda and Burundi.
Both Rwanda and Burundi are now controlled by armies from the Tutsi minority and regional analysts fear the Banyamulenge conflict could drag the region into a full-blown war.

Zaire accuses Rwanda of backing the Banyamulenge, a charge Kigali denies. Rwanda in turn accuses Zaire of supporting the 40,000-strong ethnic Hutu former army of Rwanda, overthrown by Tutsi rebels in 1994.
